whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the UX Designer exam for?

personas.label: Designers working on Salesforce projects
personas.description: You already understand user experience design and want to apply it within Salesforce, including SLDS, Lightning App Builder, and platform limits.

personas.label: Admins who have become the de facto designer
personas.description: You handle page and workflow choices for your team and want to ground those decisions in user research and accessibility practice.

personas.label: Product designers moving into enterprise software
personas.description: You are bringing product design skills into enterprise software, where people use the platform all day and many interface components follow a shared design system.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the UX Designer Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The UX Designer exam combines design practice with Salesforce configuration. Prepare for research methods, design thinking, and WCAG alongside SLDS, Lightning App Builder, and Dynamic Forms. Designers may need more platform practice; administrators may need to review research and accessibility.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
65% to pass, which is 39 correct answers out of 60.
Know the five design thinking phases and the work products associated with each one.
Review WCAG 2.1 AA, POUR, and contrast requirements: 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice matching a research question to a method and describing what its findings can establish. Also review when Lightning App Builder, Dynamic Forms, or a compact layout addresses a page requirement.

examFormat.heading: UX Designer Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or at a test center. It combines UX methods with Salesforce design features.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions present a situation and ask you to choose a research approach, identify an accessibility issue, or select a Salesforce feature that meets a page requirement.
bestWayToPass: Connect each design thinking phase to its output: research informs Empathise, a problem statement supports Define, sketches support Ideate, a model supports Prototype, and user feedback supports Test.
Memorize the WCAG details that appear in practical questions, including contrast, text alternatives, keyboard access, and visible focus.
Use Lightning App Builder to practice placing Dynamic Forms fields, configuring visibility, and editing compact layouts.
Separate methods that explain user behavior, such as interviews and usability tests, from surveys and analytics that measure patterns across a larger group.

certificationCard.description: The exam covers user research, design thinking, wireframes and prototypes, WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility, and Salesforce tools such as SLDS, Lightning App Builder, Dynamic Forms, and Experience Cloud. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 65% pass mark, weighted towards Declarative Design (27%) and Salesforce Lightning Design System (SLDS) (21%).

keyConcepts.h2: UX Designer: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: The Five Phases of Design Thinking
blocks.body: The five phases are Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test. Empathise gathers evidence through interviews, observation, personas, and journey maps. Define turns that evidence into a focused problem statement or how-might-we question. Ideate generates possible solutions, often with sketches or affinity diagrams. Prototype makes an idea tangible for feedback; Test evaluates it with users and produces findings for the next iteration. The process can move between phases as new evidence appears.

blocks.heading: Choosing a Research Method
blocks.body: Choose a research method based on the question. Interviews explore motivations, contextual inquiry observes real tasks, and usability tests uncover where an interface causes difficulty. These qualitative methods help explain why. Surveys and analytics can measure how common a behavior or opinion is. Card sorting helps users group content and informs a proposed information structure; tree testing evaluates whether users can find items in an existing structure.

blocks.heading: Wireframes, Prototypes and Handoff
blocks.body: Choose fidelity to match the decision being made. Low-fidelity sketches and wireframes help teams agree on layout before investing in detail. High-fidelity designs communicate final visual treatment. Interactive prototypes help evaluate flows and task completion. Handoff should also describe component states, empty and error cases, validation, and responsive behavior so implementation covers more than the ideal path.

blocks.heading: Accessibility: WCAG 2.1 and SLDS
blocks.body: WCAG uses four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust (POUR). Provide text alternatives, captions, and adequate contrast: at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Make interactions available from a keyboard with visible focus. Use predictable navigation, clear labels, and actionable errors. Valid markup and suitable ARIA names and roles support assistive technology. SLDS components provide an accessible baseline when their intended markup and behavior are preserved.

blocks.heading: Lightning App Builder, Dynamic Forms and the Tooling
blocks.body: Lightning App Builder arranges components on record pages and can show or hide components based on rules. Dynamic Forms lets admins place individual fields and set field visibility conditions. Dynamic Actions applies similar context rules to actions. Compact layouts determine the highlights panel and mobile preview content. Path guides users through a process with stage-specific fields and guidance. Match the requirement to the feature that controls that part of the page.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce UX Designer Exam
scenarioTips.intro: This exam asks you to apply design practice inside a platform with fixed components. The design content is mostly recall; the Salesforce content needs an hour in App Builder.

blocks.heading: Phases by Their Artefacts
blocks.body: Use the artifact named in a question to identify the relevant phase, and remember that design thinking can loop back when testing reveals a new need.

blocks.heading: WCAG Numbers
blocks.body: Review 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, along with keyboard access, visible focus, and text alternatives.

blocks.heading: Qualitative or Quantitative
blocks.body: Use interviews and usability studies to learn why; use surveys and analytics to estimate how many people show a pattern.

blocks.heading: Card Sorting Versus Tree Testing
blocks.body: Card sorting helps develop a content structure. Tree testing checks whether people can navigate a structure that already exists.

blocks.heading: Dynamic Forms and Visibility Rules
blocks.body: Practice a field visibility rule in Lightning App Builder so you can recognize when Dynamic Forms is the right tool.

sampleQuestions.question: A team interviewed users for three weeks and then wrote a problem statement. Which design thinking phase did it finish?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Define turns research findings into a clear problem statement.
whyWrong: Ideate creates possible solutions after the problem is defined.
Test checks a prototype, which has not been made yet.
Empathise is the research phase that came before the problem statement.

sampleQuestions.question: A designer wants to know whether users can find a policy in the current navigation. Which method should they use?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tree testing checks whether people can find information in an existing structure.
whyWrong: A/B testing compares two versions of something.
A survey asks people what they think; it does not show whether they can navigate.
Card sorting shows how people would group information when designing a structure.

sampleQuestions.question: Text on a custom component has a contrast ratio of 3.2:1 against its background. Which WCAG 2.1 AA rule does it fail for normal text?
options: Perceivable, because normal text needs at least 4.5:1
Robust, because grey is not a valid color
Operable, because the text cannot be clicked
sampleQuestions.explanation: Contrast is part of Perceivable. Normal-size text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.
whyWrong: Understandable is about clear, predictable content and behavior.
The stated contrast ratio is below the minimum for normal text.
Robust is about working with assistive technology; Operable is about input and controls.

sampleQuestions.question: A record page should show the Reason for Discount field only when Discount is above zero. What should the team use?
options: Dynamic Forms with a field visibility rule
A compact layout for the record highlights panel
A new record type for discount requests
A validation rule on the object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynamic Forms can show or hide a field based on a field value.
whyWrong: Compact layouts control the highlights panel, not field visibility on the form.
A new record type is more than this requirement needs.
Validation Rules check data; they do not hide fields.

sampleQuestions.question: A product owner wants to know why users abandon a multi-step form. Which research method can answer this?
options: Moderated usability testing with a small group
Sending a satisfaction survey to every user
sampleQuestions.explanation: Watching users try the task can show where they stop and why.
whyWrong: Analytics can show that users leave, but usually not why.
Support tickets only include people who report a problem and may not reveal where the form fails.
A survey can collect opinions but may not show the exact point where users get stuck.

sampleQuestions.question: A dropdown can only be opened with a mouse. Which WCAG principle does this violate?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Operable includes being able to use controls with a keyboard, not just a mouse.
whyWrong: Understandable concerns clear content and predictable behavior.
Perceivable concerns whether people can sense content, such as through text alternatives and contrast.
Robust concerns compatibility with assistive technology.

sampleQuestions.question: Why are Lightning Design System components usually a good choice for accessibility?
options: They improve performance by reducing every page load time
They cannot be customized or extended
They remove the need to follow WCAG
They include accessible markup, focus handling, and ARIA support
sampleQuestions.explanation: SLDS components include accessibility features such as suitable markup and focus handling, reducing the work needed to meet accessibility requirements.
whyWrong: Page speed is a separate concern from accessibility.
SLDS components can be themed and extended.
Teams still need to meet WCAG; SLDS helps with that work.

sampleQuestions.question: A stakeholder wants to agree on the page layout and information order before visual design begins. What should the designer create?
options: A clickable prototype with final content
sampleQuestions.explanation: Low-fidelity wireframes focus the discussion on layout and hierarchy before color and detailed styling.
whyWrong: A written document alone can make it hard to review layout.
An interactive prototype helps test a flow, which is a later step.
A detailed mock may shift the discussion to color and styling too early.

sampleQuestions.question: What can card sorting tell a designer?
options: How many users prefer a certain color
How users group and label content
Whether a page meets contrast rules
sampleQuestions.explanation: Card sorting shows how users expect related information to be grouped and labeled.
whyWrong: Usability testing checks whether people can use a prototype.
A survey can measure preferences across many people.
Contrast is checked against accessibility standards, not with card sorting.

sampleQuestions.question: A long record page overwhelms users, and different teams need different fields. What should the team try?
options: Use Dynamic Forms with field visibility rules
Create separate custom objects for each team’s fields
Train users to scroll through the long page
Remove fields that some users do not need
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynamic Forms lets the team organize fields and show them only when relevant.
whyWrong: Separate objects would split the data to solve a page-layout problem.
Training does not fix a page that is hard to use.
Removing fields could prevent other teams from doing their work.

sampleQuestions.question: Which design handoff detail is often missed and can cause implementation problems?
sampleQuestions.explanation: If a design only shows the normal, completed state, developers may have to guess what to build for empty, loading, or error situations.
whyWrong: The rationale is useful, but missing interface states can directly change what gets built.
Fonts should be specified, but the question asks for a common gap in interface behavior.
Competitor research provides background, not build details.

sampleQuestions.question: How many participants are often enough for a usability test to find recurring problems?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A small group of about five to eight participants can reveal recurring usability problems.
whyWrong: One participant may reveal a problem, but cannot show whether it recurs.
A group of 30 to 50 is more typical of a quantitative study.
Hundreds of participants are usually used for surveys or analytics, not a usability test.

sampleQuestions.question: What do Dynamic Actions control on a Salesforce record page?
options: Which buttons appear based on the record context
The highlights panel at the top of the page
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynamic Actions show the actions that fit the current record context.
whyWrong: Sharing Rules control access to records.
Field requirements are controlled by field settings or validation logic.
Compact layouts control the highlights panel.

sampleQuestions.question: A designer wants to measure how many of 4,000 users have the same navigation complaint. Which method fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A survey can measure how widespread an opinion or complaint is across a large group.
whyWrong: Usability tests show how a small group behaves and where they struggle.
Contextual inquiry closely observes a small number of people in their work setting.
Card sorting helps design or review how information is grouped.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement best describes the design thinking phases?
options: They are iterative, and teams can return to an earlier phase
They can happen in any order and all mean the same thing
They are optional after the first release
They follow a strict order, with each phase completed only once
sampleQuestions.explanation: Design thinking is iterative. Testing can show that a team should redefine the problem or create new ideas.
whyWrong: The phases have different purposes, even though teams may return to earlier phases.
Teams can keep learning and improving after release.
The phases are revisited; they are not a one-way process.
